title: Maintaining Muscular Function
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Musculoskeletal Injuries

headings.title: Introduction to Muscular Function and Musculoskeletal Health
headings.content: Musculoskeletal health is foundational to overall human movement, posture, and independence. For nursing students in Nigeria and globally, understanding muscular function goes beyond basic anatomy; it involves recognizing how skeletal muscles, bones, and joints work collaboratively to produce movement and maintain stability. Skeletal muscles are voluntary tissues innervated by the somatic nervous system, requiring adequate neural stimulation, blood supply, and mechanical loading to preserve their structural integrity and metabolic activity. Good musculoskeletal health allows patients to perform activities of daily living (ADLs) without fatigue or pain. When caring for patients in clinical settings, nurses must appreciate that muscular function is deeply interconnected with neurological, circulatory, and nutritional systems. Any disruption in these systems can rapidly compromise muscle health. Furthermore, cultural and environmental factors in Nigeria, such as the prevalence of physical labor or conversely, prolonged bed rest due to chronic illnesses, make nursing assessments of muscle status vital. Proactive nursing care aims to protect and sustain muscular function across the lifespan, preventing early deterioration and ensuring that patients recover their functional capacity swiftly following illness, surgery, or injury.

headings.title: Pathophysiology of Muscle Atrophy and Immobility
headings.content: Muscle atrophy and immobility present severe challenges in clinical nursing practice. When a patient is confined to bed rest or experiences prolonged immobilization due to trauma, stroke, or chronic illness, muscles lack the necessary mechanical loading and neural stimulation. Pathophysiologically, this lack of use triggers a decrease in protein synthesis and a dramatic increase in protein degradation, leading to muscle fiber shrinkage and loss of muscle mass, known as disuse atrophy. Beyond mass loss, immobilized muscles undergo fiber-type shifting, often losing fatigue-resistant slow-twitch fibers and experiencing declines in oxidative capacity. Circulation within the affected limbs also sluggishly decreases, reducing nutrient and oxygen delivery, which compounds tissue breakdown. Contractures can develop as connective tissue and scar tissue replace pliable muscle fibers, permanently limiting joint mobility. Additionally, calcium is leached from bones during immobility, increasing the risk of secondary complications like pathological fractures and hypercalcemia. For nurses practicing in Nigerian health facilities, identifying patients at risk for immobility-induced atrophy is critical. Early identification allows the nursing team to implement timely repositioning, splinting, and mobilization strategies that mitigate these destructive physiological changes and protect the patient's long-term mobility and independence.

headings.title: Assessment of Muscle Strength, Tone, and Joint Mobility
headings.content: Assessing muscle strength, tone, and joint mobility is a core competency for nurses. Muscle strength is typically evaluated using the standard Medical Research Council (MRC) scale, ranging from grade 0 (no movement) to grade 5 (normal strength against full resistance). During assessment, the nurse asks the patient to perform specific resistance movements against the nurse's hands, comparing bilateral limbs for symmetry. Muscle tone refers to the resting tension of skeletal muscle, often assessed by passively moving a limb to feel for resistance. Abnormal tone can manifest as hypotonia (flaccidity, commonly seen in lower motor neuron lesions or shock) or hypertonia (spasticity or rigidity, frequently observed in upper motor neuron disorders like stroke). Joint mobility assessment evaluates the active and passive range of motion of each joint, noting any crepitus, pain, swelling, or structural deformities. Nurses must document these findings meticulously to establish a baseline and monitor disease progression or recovery. In Nigerian clinical environments, where diagnostic imaging resources may occasionally be limited, thorough physical assessment of the musculoskeletal system remains a powerful, cost-effective tool to guide nursing diagnoses and interventions, ensuring that subtle changes in a patient's functional status are never overlooked.

headings.title: Range of Motion (ROM) Exercises in Nursing Care
headings.content: Range of Motion (ROM) exercises are essential nursing interventions designed to maintain joint flexibility, prevent contractures, and stimulate local circulation. ROM can be active, where the patient independently moves their joints through their full capacity, or passive, where the nurse or caregiver supports and moves the patient's limbs because the patient is unable to do so themselves. When performing passive ROM, the nurse must support the joint proximally and distally, moving each joint smoothly and gently through its anatomical plane without forcing it past the point of resistance or causing pain. Active-assistive ROM is another variation where the patient performs the exercise with partial assistance from the nurse. Integrating ROM exercises into daily bed baths or scheduled care routines helps prevent the stiffening of joints, preserves cartilage health by facilitating synovial fluid circulation, and reduces the risk of deep vein thrombosis through muscular pumping action. Nurses should educate family members on proper ROM techniques, especially in home-care settings across Nigeria where patients recovering from strokes are frequently managed at home. Regular execution of ROM exercises safeguards joint architecture and sets the stage for progressive rehabilitation.

headings.title: Active and Passive Rehabilitative Techniques
headings.content: Active and progressive rehabilitative techniques are vital for restoring lost muscle function and fostering functional independence. Once a patient is medically stable, nursing care transitions from passive maintenance to active rehabilitation strategies. Isometric exercises involve muscle contraction without joint movement, which is extremely useful for patients in casts or traction to prevent atrophy without disrupting healing bones. Isotonic exercises involve muscle contraction against a constant resistance through a range of motion, helping to build both strength and endurance. Progressive resistance training, under the guidance of nurses and physiotherapists, challenges the muscle with gradually increasing loads, stimulating cellular hypertrophy and neural adaptation. Functional retraining, such as bed mobility drills, sitting balance exercises, and gradual standing practice, helps rewire motor pathways, particularly in neurological conditions like stroke. Nurses play a crucial coordination role, encouraging patients during difficult therapy sessions, managing pain that might impede participation, and monitoring vital signs for signs of exhaustion or cardiovascular distress. In resource-constrained settings in Nigeria, nurses often improvise safe resistance tools (such as sandbags or water bottles) to ensure patients still achieve necessary progressive rehabilitation milestones.

headings.title: Nutritional Support for Muscle Maintenance and Recovery
headings.content: Nutritional support is an indispensable pillar in muscle maintenance and recovery. Muscle tissue is dynamically remodeled and repaired using amino acids derived from dietary proteins. When patients experience trauma, surgery, or prolonged bed rest, their bodies enter a catabolic state where muscle breakdown exceeds synthesis. Nurses must collaborate with dietitians to ensure patients receive high biological value proteins, such as eggs, lean meats, fish, dairy, or accessible local Nigerian protein sources like beans, cowpeas, and groundnuts. Adequate caloric intake is equally crucial; without sufficient carbohydrates and fats, the body will burn ingested or structural protein for energy rather than using it for muscle repair. Micronutrients, including vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium, are also essential for proper muscle contraction, neuromuscular transmission, and bone health. Hydration must not be overlooked, as water is the medium for cellular metabolism and transport of nutrients. Nurses should routinely screen for malnutrition using nutritional assessment tools, monitor daily food and fluid charts, and advocate for nutritional supplements when oral intake is inadequate. Providing proper nutrition accelerates wound healing, mitigates muscle wasting, and empowers the patient to participate effectively in physical rehabilitation.

headings.title: Preventing Complications of Immobility
headings.content: Preventing complications of immobility is a primary duty of the nursing profession. Prolonged immobility affects multiple body systems, precipitating pressure ulcers, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), atelectasis, pneumonia, and orthostatic hypotension, in addition to muscle atrophy and contractures. To counteract these risks, nurses implement systematic care plans. Turning and repositioning the patient every two hours relieves sustained pressure on bony prominences, protecting skin and underlying soft tissues. Early ambulation, even if it starts with dangling feet at the bedside, promotes venous return and lung expansion. Prophylactic measures such as anti-embolism stockings, sequential compression devices, and prescribed anticoagulant therapy help prevent blood stasis and subsequent DVT. Deep breathing and coughing exercises, combined with adequate hydration, keep respiratory secretions mobilized and prevent atelectasis. Nurses in Nigerian hospitals must remain vigilant, particularly when managing unconscious or paralyzed patients, utilizing pressure-relieving mattresses and heel protectors whenever available. By aggressively targeting these systemic threats, nurses create a safe physiological environment where muscles can be successfully maintained and rehabilitated without being derailed by secondary complications.

headings.title: Patient Education and Long-term Functional Independence
headings.content: Patient education and long-term functional independence are the ultimate goals of musculoskeletal nursing care. Hospital stays are temporary, and the success of muscle maintenance is ultimately determined by how well the patient and their family manage care at home. Nurses must provide comprehensive, culturally sensitive education regarding home exercise programs, proper body mechanics, safe transfer techniques, and the importance of balanced nutrition. Teaching family caregivers in Nigeria how to assist with daily stretching, transfers, and repositioning ensures continuity of care after discharge. Patients must be taught to recognize red-flag symptoms, such as severe joint pain, sudden swelling, increasing muscle weakness, or signs of DVT, and know when to seek professional medical help. Furthermore, nurses should discuss environmental modifications in the home, such as removing loose rugs, installing grab bars in bathrooms, and ensuring adequate lighting to prevent falls, which are a major threat to musculoskeletal integrity. By empowering patients with knowledge and practical skills, nurses foster long-term functional independence, drastically reduce readmission rates, and enhance the overall quality of life for individuals recovering from muscular impairment.
